title: DADA: Dual Averaging with Distance Adaptation
claim: Our parameter-free method matches or beats competing adaptive baselines across problem difficulty, converging fast where others stall or lag.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, log-scale convergence curves with shared legend
description: Three side-by-side line plots show convergence on a worst-case function, with the exponent p set to 2, 4 and 6 (d=10000 in each). The x-axis is the number of oracle calls, from 0 to 100,000. The y-axis is the log-scale optimality gap f(x_k*)−f*. Each panel has the same five methods: WDA in blue squares, UGM in orange circles, DoG in green triangles, Prodigy in red diamonds, and DADA in purple stars. Gridlines and a legend sit in the upper right of each panel. The DADA curve (purple) drops steeply and stays at or near the bottom in every panel. WDA stays high. Prodigy plateaus, then drops abruptly at some points. DoG and UGM decay smoothly but more slowly. In the p=2 panel DoG overlaps DADA. The eye goes first to the steep initial drop and the purple curve at the bottom.
caption: Comparison of different methods on the worst-case function.
abstract: We present a novel universal gradient method for solving convex optimization problems. Our algorithm, Dual Averaging with Distance Adaptation (DADA), is based on the classical scheme of dual averaging and dynamically adjusts its coefficients based on observed gradients and the distance between iterates and the starting point, eliminating the need for problem-specific parameters. DADA is a universal algorithm that simultaneously works for a broad spectrum of problem classes, provided the local growth of the objective function around its minimizer can be bounded. Particular examples of such problem classes are nonsmooth Lipschitz functions, Lipschitz-smooth functions, HÃ¶lder-smooth functions, functions with high-order Lipschitz derivative, quasi-self-concordant functions, and $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions. Crucially, DADA is applicable to both unconstrained and constrained problems, even when the domain is unbounded, without requiring prior knowledge of the number of iterations or desired accuracy.
